Renato, thank you for sending the plan early. Before we go through it, tell me the aspiration in one sentence. Not the plan — the aspiration.
A national commercial role, within the next two or three years. That is my aspiration, and I would rather say it out loud than have it guessed.
Good. Most people make me ask twice. And on readiness — what would the committee say about you today?
That the results and the team are there, and that the gap is English. It is the declared prerequisite, so there is nothing to argue about.
You named it before I did, and that is the whole point of this conversation. So what are you doing about it, with a date?
I started a programme in August, twice a week. And in October I am presenting to the global team for the first time, so I get the exposure as well as the practice.

The Commercial Director in Brazil. He raised it first, so he knows. I am also preparing one of my consultants as my successor, because nobody is going to shortlist a manager who cannot be replaced.

People assume that promotion decisions are made in the room where they are announced. They are not. By the time we sit down, most of it is already decided, and it was decided in ordinary weeks, by people who watched somebody work. So here is what I actually weigh. First, has this person made anybody else better? A manager who grows nobody is a manager I cannot move, because the region falls over the day they leave. Second, do they name their own gaps before I do? That single habit tells me more than any result on a slide. And third, yes, language. I am not looking for perfect English. I am looking for whether you can hold a room that is not in your own language, because every job above this one is that room, every single week. People hear that and think it is unfair. It is not a judgement about how clever you are. It is a description of the job.

I have read something like four hundred development plans, and the ones that fail all look the same. They are honest, they are thoughtful, and they have no dates. Somebody writes that they will improve their English, or build more visibility, and in March nobody can say whether it happened. A plan without a date is a wish with better formatting. The second failure is quieter. People write plans about things they cannot control. You cannot control whether a position opens next year. You can control whether you are the obvious answer on the day it does. So write the plan about your own behaviour, not about the company calendar. And the last thing, which almost nobody does. Tell your manager what you are working on, out loud, before they ask you. Not because they will be impressed, but because the person who is going to speak about you in a committee needs sentences to use, and if you give them none, they will use somebody else's.

My aspiration is a national commercial role, within the next two or three years. I know the gap already, and it is English, which is the declared prerequisite for the position. I started a programme in August and I am studying twice a week. In October I am presenting to the global team for the first time.
